(Surat an-Nas)
It has six verses and is Madani.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,﴾ ﴿the King of mankind,﴾ ﴿the God of mankind.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,﴾ ﴿the King of mankind,﴾ ﴿the God of mankind.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been recited as (qul a'udhu) with the hamzah omitted and its vowel transferred to the lam, and its parallel is: ﴿Take four of the birds﴾. Also, the reciters are unanimous on not pronouncing the imalah (vowel-inclination, imalah) in "an-nas," but it is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he used imalah in "an-nas" when it is in the position of the genitive (khafd).

The second issue: He, exalted is He, is the Lord of all created beings, but here He mentioned that He is the Lord of mankind specifically, and this is for several reasons:

The first of them: the seeking of refuge came from the evil of the one who whispers in the breasts of mankind, so it is as if it was said: I seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer into mankind, by their Lord who rules over their affairs, who is their God and their object of worship, just as some clients (mawali) cry out for help to their master, their lord and the one in charge of their affairs, when a calamity befalls them.

The second: the most noble of created beings in the world are mankind.

The third: the one commanded to seek refuge is the human being, so when a person recites this, it is as if he says: O my Lord, O my King, O my God.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the King of mankind﴾ and ﴿the God of mankind﴾ are both an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), like His saying: "the biography of Abu Hafs, ʿUmar al-Faruq." So He is first described as the Lord of mankind, then the lord may be a king or may not be, as one says: "lord of the house" and "lord of the goods." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah: 31]. Therefore He clarified it by saying: ﴿the King of mankind﴾. Then the king may be a god or may not be, so He clarified it by saying: ﴿the God of mankind﴾, because "God" (ilah) is specific to Him, glorified is He; no other shares it with Him. Also, He began with mention of the Lord, which is the name of the one who undertakes his management and reform, and this is among the first of His blessings, until He raised him and gave him intellect. Then the servant knows by proof that he is a servant owned, and He is his owner, so He followed it with mention of the sovereignty (mulk). Then, when he knew that worship is binding upon him and obligatory for him, and recognized that the one he worships deserves that worship, he recognized Him as God. Therefore He concluded with it. Also, the first thing the servant knows of his Lord is that He is the one who is obeyed because of the blessings He has bestowed, the apparent and the hidden, and this is the Lord. Then he continues to move from knowing these attributes to knowing His majesty and His independence from creation, and then knowledge of His being King is attained, because the king is the one whom others need, while he is independent of others. Then, when the servant knows Him thus, he knows that He is, in majesty and greatness, beyond the description of those who describe, and that He is the One before whose might and magnificence intellects are bewildered; then he knows Him as God.

The fourth issue: The reason for repeating the word "mankind" is that these attributes are repeated because explanatory apposition requires further clarification; and because this repetition indicates the increased nobility of mankind, since He, glorified is He, as it were, defines His essence by being Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind. Had mankind not been the most noble of His creatures, He would not have concluded His Book with defining His essence as Lord, King and God to them.

The fifth issue: "Malik an-nas" (King of mankind) is not permissible here, whereas "Malik yawm ad-din" (Owner of the Day of Judgement) is permissible in Surat al-Fatihah [al-Fatihah: 4]. The difference is that His saying ﴿by the Lord of mankind﴾ conveys that He is their owner, so the word following it must be this king, to convey that He is an owner, and along with being an owner He is a king. If it is said: Did He not say in Surat al-Fatihah: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2], then ﴿Owner of the Day of Judgement﴾, which would necessitate repetition there? We say: the wording indicates that He is Lord of the worlds, meaning the existing things at present, and that He is owner of the Day of Judgement, meaning capable of it. So there the Lord is attached to one thing and the owner to another, and repetition does not follow. But here, if He mentioned "owner," the Lord and the owner would be attached to one thing, and repetition would follow from it. So the difference is clear. Also, the permissibility of the recitations follows transmission, not analogy, and "Malik" has been recited, but only as an anomalous reading (shadhdh).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 114, verses 4–5:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From the evil of the whisperer, the retreating﴾. *Al-waswas* (the whisperer) is a noun meaning *al-waswasah* (the whispering), like *al-zilzal* meaning *al-zalzalah* (the quaking). As a verbal noun (*masdar*), it is *wiswas* with a kasra, like *zilzal*. The word here refers to Satan, who is named by the verbal noun as though he were the whispering itself, because whispering is his craft and the occupation to which he is devoted. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is one whose conduct is not righteous﴾ [Hud: 46], where the meaning is "the one possessing" (the conduct). The full discussion of whispering has already been given under His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. As for *al-Khannas* (the retreating), it is one whose habit is to withdraw (*yakhnis*), a form attributed to *al-khunus*, which means retreating, like *al-'awwaj* and *al-naffathat*. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "When a person remembers his Lord, Satan withdraws and turns away; but when he is heedless, Satan whispers to him."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿who whispers﴾ may take any of the three vowel states (*harakat*) in its grammatical position. The genitive (*al-jarr*) is used as a qualifier (*al-sifah*) of the preceding word, while the nominative (*al-raf'*) and accusative (*al-nasb*) are used by way of vituperation (*al-shatm*, dispraise of the one being described). It is also good for the reciter to pause at *al-Khannas* and begin with *alladhi yuwaswisu* ("who whispers"), according to either of these two readings.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿who whispers﴾ may take any of the three vowel states (*harakat*) in its grammatical position. The genitive (*al-jarr*) is used as a qualifier (*al-sifah*) of the preceding word, while the nominative (*al-raf'*) and accusative (*al-nasb*) are used by way of vituperation (*al-shatm*, dispraise of the one being described). It is also good for the reciter to pause at *al-Khannas* and begin with *alladhi yuwaswisu* ("who whispers"), according to either of these two readings.

Regarding His saying, ﴿From among the jinn and mankind﴾, there are several opinions:

First: It is as if He says: the whisperer who withdraws (al-waswas al-khannas) may be from the jinn and may be from mankind, just as He said: ﴿Satans of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. Just as the satan of the jinn sometimes whispers and sometimes withdraws, so too the satan of mankind is like this. That is because he sees himself as a sincere and compassionate advisor: if the listener rebukes him, he withdraws and abandons the whispering; and if the listener accepts his words, he goes to excess in it.

Second: Some people said: His saying ﴿from among the jinn and mankind﴾ refers to two categories falling under His saying ﴿in the breasts of mankind﴾, as if the common element between the jinn and humans is called "insan" (human), and the human is also called "insan," so the word "insan" applies to the genus and the species by way of shared usage. The evidence that the word "insan" includes both the jinn and humans is what is narrated: that a group of jinn came and it was said to them: "Who are you?" and they said: "Unas (people) from among the jinn." Also, God called them "rijal" (men) in His saying: ﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6]. So it is permissible also to call them "nas" (people) here. The meaning of the verse on this interpretation is that this whisperer who withdraws is extremely prone to withdrawing; he does not limit himself to misguiding humans but misguides his own kind, who are the jinn; so it is fitting for the intelligent person to beware of his evil. This opinion, however, is weak, because making "insan" a name for the genus that includes both jinn and humans is far from linguistic usage: the jinn were named "jinn" because of their concealment (ijtinan), and the human was named "insan" because of his visibility from "al-iynas," which is seeing. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Whoever wishes to establish this interpretation, it is preferable to say: what is meant by His saying ﴿whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾ is: in the breasts of people, like His saying ﴿the Day the caller calls﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. And if what is meant by 'nas' is 'the forgetful' (al-nasi), then it is possible to divide it into jinn and humans, since they are the two kinds described as forgetting the right of God Most High."

Third: The meaning may be: "I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind from the whisperer who withdraws, and from the jinn and mankind," as if he sought refuge with his Lord from that one satan, then sought refuge with his Lord from all of them: the jinn and mankind.

Know that in this surah there is another subtle point: the one sought refuge with in the first surah is mentioned with one attribute, namely that He is the Lord of the daybreak (rabb al-falaq), and the things sought refuge from are three kinds of harms: the darkness when it settles (al-ghasiq), the blowers in knots (al-naffathat), and the envier (al-hasid). In this surah, however, the one sought refuge with is mentioned with three attributes: Lord, King, and God (al-Rabb, al-Malik, al-Ilah), and the thing sought refuge from is one harm, namely the whispering (al-waswasa). The difference between the two places is that praise must be proportioned to the extent of what is sought: what is sought in the first surah is the safety of the self and body, and what is sought in the second surah is the safety of religion. This is an alert that the harm to religion, however small, is greater than the harms of this world, however great. And God, glory be to Him, knows best.

End.
